title: Phaedo and Polemo
source_text: Εἰκὸς δ᾿ αὐτὸν τοιοῦτον βούλεσθαι δηλοῦν, ὅτι τοὺς πρὸς τὰ τοιάδε ἁμαρτήματα καὶ γινόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν ἐξωλεστάτων οὐ μόνον πεφυκότας ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰθισμένους οὐδεὶς αν οὐδὲ κολάζων πάντῃ μεταβάλοι. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ψεῦδος ἀπὸ τῆς περί τινων φιλοσοφησάντων ἱστορίας ἀποδείκνυται. τίς γὰρ ἀνθρώπων οὐκ ἂν ἐν τοῖς ἐξωλεστάτοις τάσσοι τὸν ὅπως ποτὲ ὑπομείναντα εἶξαι δεσπότῃ, ἐπὶ τέγους αὐτὸν ἱστάντι, ἵνα πάντα τὸν θέλοντα αὐτὸν καταισχύνειν παραδέξηται; τοιαῦτα δὲ περὶ τοῦ Φαίδωνος ἱστορεῖται. τίς δὲ τὸν μετὰ αὐλητρίδος καὶ κωμαστῶν τῶν συνασωτευσαμένων εἰσβαλόντα εἰς τὴν τοῦ σεμνοτάτου Ξενοκράτους διατριβὴν, ἵν᾿ ἐνυβρίσῃ ἄνδρα, ὃν καὶ οἱ ἑταῖροι ἐθαύμαζον, οὐ φήσει πάντων μιαρώτατον εἶναι ἀνθρώπων; ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως ἴσχυσε λόγος καὶ τούτους ἐπιστρέψας ποιῆσαι ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον διαβεβηκέναι ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ. ὥστε τὸν μὲν ὑπὸ Πλάτωνος κριθῆναι ἄξιον τοῦ τὸν περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας διεξοδεῦσαι Σωκράτους λόγον καὶ τὴν ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ εὐτονίαν αὐτοῦ παραστῆσαι, οὐ φροντίσαντος τοῦ κωνείου ἀλλ᾿ ἀδεῶς καὶ μετὰ πάσης γαλήνης τῆς ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ διεξοδεύσαντος τοσαῦτα καὶ τηλικαῦτα, οἷς μόγις παρακολουθεῖν καὶ οἱ πάνυ καθεστηκότες καὶ ὑπὸ μηδεμιᾶς ἐνοχλούμενοι περιστάσεως δύνανται· τὸν δὲ Πολέμωνα, ἐξ ἀσώτου γενόμενον σωφρονέστατον, διαδέξασθαι τὴν τοῦ διαβοήτου ἐπὶ σεμνότητι Ξενοκράτους διατριβήν. οὐκ ἄρα ἀληθεύει Κέλσος λέγων τοὺς πεφυκότας ἁμαρτάνειν καὶ εἰθισμένους οὐδεὶς ἂν οὐδὲ κολάζων πάντῃ μεταβάλοι.
pass_a_gloss: It is likely (εἰκός) that he wishes to show (δηλόω) some such thing: that those not only by nature but also accustomed toward such and such sins, ones done by the most abandoned (ἐξωλέστατος), no one even punishing would wholly change. And this too is shown (ἀποδείκνυμι) false (ψεῦδος) from the history (ἱστορία) about certain men who philosophised. For who of men would not rank (τάσσω) among the most abandoned the one who somehow (ὅπως ποτέ) endured (ὑπομένω) to yield (εἴκω) to a master (δεσπότης) setting him in a brothel (ἐπὶ τέγους, τέγος), so that he might receive (παραδέχομαι) everyone wishing to shame (καταισχύνω) him? Such things are recorded about Phaedo. And who will not say that he who with a flute-girl (αὐλητρίς) and revellers (κωμαστής) who joined in profligacy (συνασωτεύομαι) burst into (εἰσβάλλω) the school (διατριβή) of the most venerable (σεμνότατος) Xenocrates, to insult (ἐνυβρίζω) a man whom even the companions (ἑταῖρος) admired, is most foul (μιαρώτατος) of all men? But nevertheless reason/word (λόγος) prevailed (ἰσχύω), having turned (ἐπιστρέφω) these too, to make them advance (διαβαίνω, pf.) so far in philosophy that the one was judged by Plato worthy to go through (διεξοδεύω) the discourse of Socrates about immortality (ἀθανασία) and to present his firmness (εὐτονία) in the prison (δεσμωτήριον), he not caring (φροντίζω) for the hemlock (κώνειον) but fearlessly (ἀδεῶς) and with all calm (γαλήνη) in the soul going through so many and such great things, which hardly (μόγις) even those quite settled (καθίστημι, pf.) and troubled (ἐνοχλέω) by no circumstance (περίστασις) can follow (παρακολουθέω); and Polemo, from profligate (ἄσωτος) become most self-controlled (σωφρονέστατος), succeeded to (διαδέχομαι) the school of Xenocrates, famed (διαβόητος) for dignity (σεμνότης). Celsus then does not speak truth (ἀληθεύω), saying that those by nature sinning and accustomed no one even punishing would wholly change.
pass_b_english: It is likely that he means something like this: that no one could completely change, not even by punishing them, those who are not only naturally inclined but also accustomed to sins of this kind, the sort committed by the most abandoned. This too is shown to be false from the history of certain men who became philosophers. For who would not rank among the most abandoned the man who somehow brought himself to submit to a master who put him in a brothel, so that he would receive anyone who wished to shame him? Such things are told of Phaedo. And who will not say that the vilest of all men was the one who burst into the school of the most venerable Xenocrates with a flute-girl and a band of revellers who shared his debauchery, to insult a man whom even his companions admired?

Yet teaching had the power to turn even these men and to make them advance so far in philosophy that the one was judged by Plato worthy to recount Socrates' discourse on immortality and to portray his steadfastness in prison: how he paid no heed to the hemlock, but fearlessly, with complete calm of soul, discussed matters so many and so great that even those who are thoroughly composed and troubled by no circumstance can hardly follow them; and the other, Polemo, turning from a profligate into a man of the greatest self-control, succeeded to the school of Xenocrates, a man renowned for his dignity. So Celsus does not speak the truth when he says that no one could completely change those who are naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it, not even by punishing them.

choices.choice: No Scripture quotation or clear allusion; no classical quotation, so no inline classical citation. The stories of Phaedo (sold into slavery and put in a brothel, later ransomed into Socrates' circle) and of Polemo (the drunken reveller converted by Xenocrates' lecture) are known also from Diogenes Laertius 2.105 and 4.16; not cited inline because Origen does not quote them. The 'discourse on immortality' is Plato's Phaedo, narrated by Phaedo; not cited inline because it is a reference, not a quotation. ἐπὶ τέγους: τέγος is a room, specifically a brothel (LSJ). 'Whom even his companions admired' (ὃν καὶ οἱ ἑταῖροι ἐθαύμαζον): the Greek does not say whose companions, Xenocrates' or the reveller's; the English keeps the ambiguity. λόγος in 'teaching had the power' (anarthrous) is the persuasive discourse of philosophy, which 3.68 calls 'philosophical discourses' (τῶν ἀπὸ φιλοσοφίας λόγων); it is not the divine Word, so it is rendered 'teaching' and left lowercase. αν in οὐδεὶς αν is a source typo for ἄν. The TEI full stop after φιλοσοφίᾳ breaks the result clause (ὥστε ...); read as continuous, with both τὸν μέν (Phaedo) and τὸν δὲ Πολέμωνα kept inside it.
λόγος: 'reason had the power' -> 'teaching had the power' (the philosophical discourse that 3.68 names; 'reason' misread the point)
Polemo clause restored inside the ὥστε result clause ('and the other, Polemo, turning ... succeeded'), as the Greek τὸν μὲν ... τὸν δέ requires
'renowned for his dignity' now clearly Xenocrates ('a man renowned for his dignity')
'his fellows' -> 'his companions' (ἑταῖροι; 'fellows' was dated and unclear)
Celsus's repeated sentence put in natural English order, 'not even by punishing'
